core.p: Unit pricing compares the cost of items of different sizes to find the best value for money. To compare items, calculate the cost per single unit, such as price per 100g, price per 1L, or price per single item.
bullets: Divide the total cost by the total quantity to find the unit price.
Always compare using the exact same unit of measurement.
The best buy is the option with the lowest unit price.
Check if multi-packs actually offer savings compared to single items.

callouts.p: Convert all quantities to either 100g or 1kg before comparing prices.

core.p: Rates of pay calculate earnings over a specified time period. Common examples include hourly rates, piece-work rates, and annual salaries divided into weekly or monthly blocks.
bullets: Total pay = Hourly rate x Number of hours worked.
Overtime usually pays a higher rate, such as time-and-a-half.
To find the hourly rate, divide total earnings by total hours.
Be careful with minutes when calculating fractional hours.

callouts.p: 30 minutes is 0.5 hours, not 0.3 hours! 15 minutes is 0.25 hours.

core.p: Time does not follow the decimal base-10 system, which makes working with compound units tricky. There are 60 seconds in a minute and 60 minutes in an hour. Converting time to decimals is essential before multiplying or dividing.
bullets: To convert minutes to a decimal of an hour, divide by 60.
Example: 45 minutes = 45 / 60 = 0.75 hours.
Never multiply time in minutes directly by a decimal speed without converting.
Double-check your final time units.

core.p: Higher tariff Foundation questions combine two or more compound units. For example, calculating the total cost of fuel for a journey requires knowing distance, speed, fuel consumption rate, and cost per litre.
bullets: Break complex problems down into step-by-step calculations.
Write down intermediate answers clearly with their units.
Check that your final answer makes physical sense.
Ensure all unit conversions are completed before performing calculations.

callouts.p: Check that the units cancel out properly during multiplication to leave the required unit.

core.p: Sometimes exam questions ask you to convert a compound unit from one metric form to another, such as converting metres per second into kilometres per hour, or grams per cubic centimetre into kilograms per cubic metre.
bullets: Convert the numerator and denominator separately.
To convert m/s to km/h, multiply by 3.6.
To convert km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6.
Write out conversion factors step by step to avoid errors.

core.p: Some problems require working backwards from a compound unit. If you are given the speed and the time, you must calculate the distance. If you are given the density and volume, you must find the mass.
bullets: Identify the target variable from the question wording.
Select the correct rearranged formula.
Substitute known values carefully.
Include correct units in your final answer line.

callouts.p: Isolating an unknown variable in an equation by applying inverse operations.

analogy.p: Think of compound units like baking a cake where the recipe calls for flour and sugar in a strict ratio, or combining ingredients at a specific rate per person. If you change the number of people (time/volume), you must scale all other parts proportionally using the compound formula. This analogy breaks down because physical laws like speed and density have hard limits and exact universal constants, whereas recipes can be adjusted freely to taste.

terms.d: A unit of measurement formed by combining two or more base units through multiplication or division.
The rate of change of distance with respect to time, calculated as distance divided by time.
The mass of a substance per unit volume, calculated as mass divided by volume.
The force applied perpendicular to the surface of an object per unit area.
The cost of a commodity per given unit of weight, volume, or count.
The amount of money earned per unit of time worked.
A measure of the amount of matter in an object, typically measured in grams or kilograms.
The amount of three-dimensional space occupied by an object or substance.
A push or pull upon an object resulting from its interaction with another object, measured in Newtons.
The quantity that expresses the extent of a two-dimensional figure or shape, measured in square units.
The SI derived unit of pressure, equivalent to one Newton per square metre.
A measure of how one quantity changes in relation to another quantity.

mistakes.w: Writing time as a standard decimal without converting minutes (e.g. writing 2 hours 30 minutes as 2.30).
mistakes.r: Convert minutes to a fraction of an hour by dividing by 60 (2.5 hours).

mistakes.w: Using the wrong formula triangle arrangement, such as dividing speed by distance.
mistakes.r: Always check the formula triangle: Distance is at the top, Speed and Time are at the bottom.

mistakes.w: Comparing unit prices using different units of measure, such as comparing 500g against 1kg directly.
mistakes.r: Convert all quantities to the exact same unit before comparing prices.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to include compound units in the final answer line.
mistakes.r: Always write the correct units (e.g., m/s, g/cm cubed, N/m squared).

mistakes.w: Multiplying speed by time when time is given in minutes without dividing by 60 first.
mistakes.r: Ensure time is in hours if speed is in miles per hour or km/h.

mistakes.w: Confusing mass and volume in density calculations.
mistakes.r: Density = Mass / Volume. Mass is on top, Volume is on the bottom.

mistakes.w: Dividing area by force when calculating pressure.
mistakes.r: Pressure = Force / Area. Force is on top, Area is on the bottom.

exam.q: A train travels 180 miles in 2 hours and 30 minutes. Work out the average speed of the train in miles per hour.
model: Converts 30 minutes to 0.5 hours (or states 2.5 hours)
Correct answer of 72 mph with units
exam.tip: Always convert time into decimal hours before dividing distance by time.

exam.q: A solid metal block has a mass of 540g and a volume of 200cm cubed. Calculate the density of the block.
exam.tip: State the formula clearly before substituting numbers.

exam.q: A box exerts a force of 120 Newtons on a table. The area of contact is 0.4 m squared. Work out the pressure on the table.
model: Correct answer of 300 N/m squared (or Pascals)
exam.tip: Remember Force is always on top of the pressure formula.

exam.q: Pack A has 400g of cereal for £2.40. Pack B has 750g of cereal for £4.20. Which pack is better value for money? You must show your working.
model: Finds unit price for Pack A: £2.40 / 4 = £0.60 per 100g (or 0.6p per gram)
Finds unit price for Pack B: £4.20 / 7.5 = £0.56 per 100g
Concludes Pack B is better value with supporting figures
exam.tip: Find the cost per 100g for both items to make a clear comparison.

exam.q: Convert a speed of 72 km/h into metres per second.
exam.tip: Memorise that km/h to m/s requires dividing by 3.6.

exam.q: A cyclist travels at an average speed of 12 m/s for 45 minutes. What distance does the cyclist travel in metres?
model: Converts 45 minutes to seconds: 45 x 60 = 2700 seconds (or converts speed to m/min)
Uses Distance = Speed x Time: 12 x 2700
exam.tip: Match your time units to your speed units before multiplying.

exam.q: Liquid A has a density of 0.8 g/cm cubed. 300cm cubed of Liquid A is mixed with 200cm cubed of Liquid B. Liquid B has a density of 1.2 g/cm cubed. Work out the density of the mixture.
model: Calculates mass of Liquid A: 0.8 x 300 = 240g
Calculates mass of Liquid B: 1.2 x 200 = 240g
Calculates total mass (480g) and total volume (500cm cubed)
exam.tip: For mixed substances, find total mass and total volume separately.

exam.q: Work out the mass of a block of wood with a volume of 250 cm cubed and a density of 0.6 g/cm cubed.
exam.tip: Use the density triangle to confirm Mass = Density multiplied by Volume.

exam.q: A force of 45 N is applied to an area of 150 cm squared. Calculate the pressure in N/m squared.
model: Converts area to m squared: 150 cm squared = 0.015 m squared (or recognises conversion trap)
exam.tip: Watch out for area given in cm squared when pressure requires m squared.

exam.q: Jemma works 35 hours a week and is paid £11.20 per hour. She also works 4 hours of overtime at time-and-a-half. Calculate her total weekly pay.
model: Adds both for total pay of £459.20
exam.tip: Calculate standard pay and overtime pay separately before adding them together.

worked.q: A car travels 210 miles in 3 hours 15 minutes. Calculate the average speed of the car in miles per hour.
steps: Convert the time into decimal hours: 15 minutes = 15 / 60 = 0.25 hours, so time = 3.25 hours.
State the speed formula: Speed = Distance / Time.
Substitute the values: Speed = 210 / 3.25.
Calculate the final answer: 64.615... mph.

worked.q: A gold-coloured statue has a mass of 1930g and a volume of 100 cm cubed. Given that pure gold has a density of 19.3 g/cm cubed, determine whether the statue is made of pure gold.
steps: Recall the density formula: Density = Mass / Volume.
Substitute the given mass and volume: Density = 1930 / 100.
Perform the division: Density = 19.3 g/cm cubed.
Compare with the density of pure gold and conclude.
worked.ans: Yes, the density matches 19.3 g/cm cubed exactly, so it could be pure gold.

maths_aqa_f.2.2.summary: Expressing one quantity as a fraction of another is the foundation of ratio work in AQA Foundation Maths. It means writing how many parts of one quantity fit into a second, using the form \(\frac{a}{b}\). This skill underpins later topics such as scale factors, percentages and direct proportion, and the exam expects you to simplify fractions, interpret the meaning of the fraction and use it in real‑world contexts.

core.h: What does ‘express as a fraction of’ mean?
core.p: You are asked to write the relationship between two quantities as a fraction \(\frac{part}{whole}\). The numerator is the amount you are comparing, the denominator is the reference amount.
bullets: Identify the two quantities given in the question.
Decide which quantity is the part (the one you are measuring) and which is the whole (the reference).
Write the fraction in the form \(\frac{part}{whole}\).

callouts.p: To write one quantity as a fraction of another means to represent the first quantity divided by the second, i.e. \(\frac{first}{second}\).

core.h: Choosing the correct part and whole
core.p: The wording of the question tells you which quantity is the part. Look for key verbs such as ‘of’, ‘per’, ‘each’, ‘out of’, or ‘as a proportion of’.
bullets: ‘How many metres are in 5 km?’ → part = metres, whole = kilometres.
‘What fraction of the class are girls?’ → part = number of girls, whole = total pupils.

callouts.p: If you are unsure, write both possible fractions and check which one makes sense in the context.

core.p: All AQA answers must be in lowest terms unless the question explicitly asks for a decimal or percentage.
bullets: Find the greatest common divisor (GCD) of numerator and denominator.
Divide both by the GCD.
Check that the denominator is not 1 unless the answer is a whole number.

callouts.p: Do not leave the fraction unsimplified – marks are lost for not reducing.

core.p: A fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) is exactly the same as the ratio \(a:b\). This equivalence is useful when the exam asks for a ratio after you have found a fraction.
bullets: If \(\frac{3}{5}\) is obtained, the equivalent ratio is 3:5.
Both forms convey the same relationship; choose the one the question requires.

callouts.p: A fraction and a ratio are interchangeable – remember this when converting.

core.h: Using the fraction in a real‑world context
core.p: After you have the fraction, interpret it: it tells you how many units of the part are contained in each unit of the whole.
bullets: \(\frac{250}{1000}=\frac{1}{4}\) means 1 litre of juice is ¼ of a 4‑litre bottle.
In a speed problem, \(\frac{30\,\text{km}}{2\,\text{h}}=15\,\text{km/h}\) – the fraction gives the rate.

core.h: Common units and conversion before forming the fraction
core.p: If the two quantities are in different units, convert them first so the fraction is dimensionally consistent.
bullets: Convert km to metres, minutes to seconds, etc.
Only then write \(\frac{part}{whole}\).

callouts.p: A common exam trap is to write the fraction before converting – always check units first.

core.h: Fraction of a whole versus percentage
core.p: A fraction can be turned into a percentage by multiplying by 100. The exam may ask for either form.
bullets: If the question says ‘express as a fraction’, do not give the percentage unless asked.

core.p: Use a quick sanity check: does the fraction make sense in the context?
bullets: If the part is larger than the whole, the fraction should be >1 (or an improper fraction).
If the part is a subset, the fraction should be <1.

analogy.p: Think of a whole pizza as the ‘whole’ quantity. Each slice you take is the ‘part’. Expressing the part as a fraction of the whole is like saying ‘I have 2 slices out of 8’, i.e. \(\frac{2}{8}=\frac{1}{4}\). The analogy breaks down when the pizza is cut into unequal slices – in maths the part must be measured in the same units as the whole.

terms.d: A numerical expression of the form \(\frac{numerator}{denominator}\) representing one quantity divided by another.
The quantity being compared or measured; the numerator in the fraction.
The reference quantity; the denominator in the fraction.
Reduce a fraction to its lowest terms by dividing numerator and denominator by their greatest common divisor.
A comparison of two quantities expressed as \(a:b\) which is equivalent to the fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\).
Changing a measurement from one unit to another (e.g., km to m) so that both quantities are comparable.
A fraction multiplied by 100, giving a value per hundred.
A fraction where the numerator is larger than the denominator, representing a value greater than 1.
The largest integer that divides both numerator and denominator exactly.
A fraction whose numerator and denominator share no common factors other than 1.
A quick reasoning step to confirm the answer makes sense in the context.
Having both numerator and denominator expressed in the same units before forming a fraction.

mistakes.w: The fraction is 5/3 because 3 km is larger than 5 km.
mistakes.r: The part must be the smaller quantity when the question asks ‘what fraction of the larger is the smaller’; the correct fraction is \(\frac{3}{5}\).

mistakes.w: I left the fraction 12/18 unsimplified.
mistakes.r: Mark scheme requires the fraction in lowest terms – simplify to \(\frac{2}{3}\).

mistakes.w: I wrote 0.6 instead of 3/5 because the question asked for a fraction.
mistakes.r: If the question explicitly says ‘express as a fraction’, give \(\frac{3}{5}\), not the decimal.

mistakes.w: I converted km to miles before forming the fraction because I thought it looked nicer.
mistakes.r: Convert only when the question requires the same units; unnecessary conversion can introduce errors.

mistakes.w: I wrote the ratio 5:3 instead of the fraction 5/3.
mistakes.r: The exam may ask for a fraction; a ratio is not acceptable unless requested.

mistakes.w: I multiplied the numerator and denominator by 2 to get 6/10 and thought it was simpler.
mistakes.r: Multiplying makes the fraction larger; only division by the GCD simplifies.

mistakes.w: I assumed the fraction must always be less than 1.
mistakes.r: Improper fractions (>1) are valid when the part exceeds the whole, e.g., 9/4 metres is 2¼ metres.

mistakes.w: I wrote 25% instead of 1/4 because I remembered the percentage rule.
mistakes.r: The question asked for a fraction; give \(\frac{1}{4}\).

mistakes.w: I ignored the units and wrote 250/1000 as 250/1000.
mistakes.r: Units must be the same before forming the fraction; after conversion the simplified fraction is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

mistakes.w: I wrote the answer as 4/1 because I thought the whole should be first.
mistakes.r: The part is always the numerator; the whole is the denominator. The correct fraction is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

exam.q: A school has 120 pupils, of which 45 are boys. Express the number of boys as a fraction of the total number of pupils.
model: Identify part = boys (45) and whole = total pupils (120).
Write fraction 45/120 and simplify by GCD 15 → 3/8.
exam.tip: Check you have simplified fully; 45/120 → 3/8.

exam.q: A recipe uses 250 g of sugar for 1 kg of flour. Write the amount of sugar as a fraction of the amount of flour.
model: Convert 1 kg to 1000 g so units match.
exam.tip: Always convert to the same unit before forming the fraction.

exam.q: A car travels 150 km in 3 h. Express the distance travelled as a fraction of the time taken.
model: Part = distance (150 km), whole = time (3 h).
Explain that the fraction represents 50 km per hour, i.e. a rate.
exam.tip: If the fraction reduces to a whole number, it is still a valid answer.

exam.q: In a bag there are 8 red marbles and 12 blue marbles. Express the number of red marbles as a fraction of the total number of marbles.
exam.tip: Add the two quantities first to get the whole.

exam.q: A shop sells 45 pens in a box that holds 60 pens. Write the number of pens sold as a fraction of the box capacity.
exam.tip: Remember to simplify.

exam.q: A runner completes 9 laps of a 400 m track. Express the distance run as a fraction of a kilometre.
model: Convert kilometre to metres: 1 km = 1000 m.
exam.tip: Improper fractions are acceptable; you may also give the mixed number 3 ⅖ if you wish.

exam.q: A bottle contains 750 ml of juice. Express the volume of juice as a fraction of a litre.
model: Convert litre to ml: 1 L = 1000 ml.
exam.tip: Unit conversion first, then simplify.

exam.q: A class has 30 students. 18 of them scored above 80%. Write the number scoring above 80% as a fraction of the class.
exam.tip: Check the fraction is in lowest terms.

exam.q: A garden is 12 m long and 9 m wide. Express the length as a fraction of the width.
exam.tip: Improper fraction shows length is larger than width.

worked.q: Express 250 g of sugar as a fraction of 2 kg of flour.
steps: Convert 2 kg to grams: 2 kg = 2000 g.
Write fraction 250 g / 2000 g = 250/2000.

worked.q: A school has 180 pupils, 72 of whom are girls. Write the number of girls as a fraction of the total pupils.
steps: Part = 72, whole = 180.
Fraction = 72/180.

worked.q: A cyclist rides 45 km in 1.5 h. Express the distance as a fraction of the time.
steps: Convert 1.5 h to a fraction: 1.5 = 3/2 hours.

maths_aqa_f.2.4.summary: Dividing a quantity in a given ratio means sharing a whole into parts that have the same relative size as the numbers in the ratio. By converting the ratio into a unit‑fraction you can work out each part quickly, then apply it to real‑world situations such as recipes, maps, speed and pricing. Mastery of this skill lets you interpret and solve a wide range of GCSE questions, from simple sharing problems to more complex word‑problems involving rates of change.

core.p: A ratio compares two or more quantities of the same kind, showing how many times one value contains another.
bullets: Written as a:b, a:b:c … or using the word ‘to’ (a to b).
Both numbers must be in the same units before forming the ratio.
The order matters – a:b is not the same as b:a.

callouts.p: A ratio is a relationship between two or more numbers that indicates how many times one quantity contains another.

core.h: Reducing a ratio to its simplest form
core.p: Simplify by dividing all terms by their greatest common divisor (GCD). This does not change the relationship, only makes calculations easier.
bullets: Find the GCD of all terms.
Divide each term by the GCD.
Resulting numbers are the simplest whole‑number ratio.

callouts.p: If a ratio contains a zero, the whole ratio cannot be simplified – keep the zero as a term.

core.h: Converting a ratio into a unit‑fraction
core.p: A unit‑fraction tells you the size of one part of the whole when the whole is split according to the ratio.
bullets: Add all the terms of the ratio to get the total number of equal parts.
One part = 1 ÷ (sum of terms).
Multiply this unit‑fraction by the required quantity to get the size of each part.

callouts.p: Unit‑fraction = 1 / (a + b + …) for a:b:…

core.h: Step‑by‑step method to divide a quantity
core.p: Follow these five clear steps for any exam question.
bullets: 1️⃣ Write the given ratio in simplest whole‑number form.
2️⃣ Add the terms to find the total number of parts.
3️⃣ Find the size of one part: required quantity ÷ total parts.
4️⃣ Multiply the size of one part by each term of the ratio.
5️⃣ Check that the parts add back to the original quantity.

callouts.p: Never forget to convert units first – mixing metres with centimetres will give a wrong ratio.

core.p: A £120 prize is to be shared between three friends in the ratio 4:3:5. Find each share.

core.p: A cyclist travels 30 km in the time it takes a car to travel 45 km. The distance ratio is 30:45. Find the speed of the cyclist if the car’s speed is 60 km h⁻¹.

callouts.p: Speed is a rate – distance ÷ time. The same time means the ratio of distances equals the ratio of speeds.

core.p: The question will usually tell you the total amount and the ratio, or sometimes give you one part and ask for the whole.
bullets: "A sum of money is to be divided in the ratio …"
"If the ratio of A:B is 4:5 and B receives £150, find A."
"The mixture contains ingredients in the ratio 3:2. Find the amount of each if the total is 45 g."

callouts.p: When only one part is given, first find the size of one part, then multiply to get the whole.

core.p: Always verify that the parts add back to the original quantity and that the ratio of the parts matches the given ratio.
bullets: Add the calculated parts – should equal the total.
Divide any two parts – should simplify to the original ratio.
Re‑state the answer with correct units.

core.p: Dividing a quantity in a ratio is the reverse of finding a ratio from two quantities; both use the same simplification skills.
bullets: R4 – using ratio notation and simplifying.
R6 – expressing a multiplicative relationship as a ratio.
R7 – recognising proportion as equality of two ratios.
**One part** = Total ÷ (sum of ratio terms)
**Part i** = (ratio term i) × One part
**Total** = Σ (ratio term × One part)

analogy.p: Imagine a pizza cut into slices that represent the numbers in a ratio – 4 slices for Alice, 2 for Ben, 3 for Cara. The whole pizza is the total quantity. By counting the total slices you know the size of one slice, then you can give each person the correct number of slices. The analogy breaks down when the ‘pizza’ is not a single, divisible whole (e.g., when dealing with rates of change where time is involved) or when the slices must be of different sizes – in those cases you need to use unit‑fractions rather than equal slices.

terms.d: A relationship between two or more quantities of the same kind, expressed as a:b or a to b.
A ratio where the terms have no common factor greater than 1.
The value of one part when a whole is divided into a number of equal parts equal to the sum of the ratio terms.
An equality of two ratios, written as a:b = c:d.
The multiplier that changes one quantity to another in the same ratio.
When one quantity increases, the other increases at a constant rate; expressed as y = kx.
When one quantity increases, the other decreases such that their product is constant; expressed as y = k/x.
A unit formed from two different units, e.g., km h⁻¹, £ kg⁻¹.
The amount by which a quantity changes per unit of another quantity, often expressed as a ratio.
The sum of all terms in a ratio, representing the number of equal shares the whole is divided into.
The amount of the whole allocated to one term of the ratio.
A method for checking proportion: a·d = b·c for a:b = c:d.

mistakes.w: I divided the total by the number of terms, not by the sum of the terms.
mistakes.r: You must divide by the sum of the ratio terms (total parts), not by how many terms there are.

mistakes.w: I left the ratio unsimplified and got a decimal answer.
mistakes.r: Simplify the ratio first; the unit‑fraction is based on the simplest whole‑number ratio.

mistakes.w: I mixed units (e.g., km with m) before forming the ratio.
mistakes.r: Convert all quantities to the same unit before writing the ratio.

mistakes.w: I added the ratio terms incorrectly (e.g., 4+2+3 = 8 instead of 9).
mistakes.r: Check the addition of all ratio terms; the total parts must be accurate.

mistakes.w: I multiplied the total by each ratio term instead of dividing first.
mistakes.r: Find the size of one part (total ÷ total parts) before multiplying by each term.

mistakes.w: I gave the answer in the wrong unit (e.g., £ instead of kg).
mistakes.r: Keep the original unit for each share; only the size changes, not the unit.

mistakes.w: I assumed the ratio could be written as a fraction directly (e.g., 3/5 of total).
mistakes.r: Only do this after converting the ratio to a unit‑fraction; 3/5 is only correct if the sum of terms is 5.

mistakes.w: I forgot to check that the parts add back to the total.
mistakes.r: Always add the calculated shares to confirm they equal the original quantity.

mistakes.w: I used the ratio the wrong way round (e.g., 5:3 instead of 3:5).
mistakes.r: Maintain the order given in the question; swapping changes the meaning.

mistakes.w: I rounded intermediate steps and lost marks.
mistakes.r: Keep calculations exact until the final answer; only round if the question asks for a certain number of significant figures.

exam.q: A total of 840 g of a metal alloy is made by mixing metals A and B in the ratio 7:5. Find the mass of each metal.
exam.tip: Remember to check that 490 g + 350 g = 840 g.

exam.q: The ratio of the speeds of two cyclists is 3:4. If the slower cyclist travels at 12 km h⁻¹, find the speed of the faster cyclist.
exam.tip: Speed ratio equals distance ratio when time is the same.

exam.q: A recipe calls for sugar, butter and flour in the ratio 2:3:5. If you have 600 g of flour, how much sugar and butter are needed?
model: Flour corresponds to the third term (5).
Check: 240 g + 360 g + 600 g = 1200 g total.
exam.tip: Identify which term of the ratio the given quantity represents.

exam.q: A sum of £560 is to be divided between three people in the ratio 5:4:6. Find each person's share.
exam.tip: Use a calculator for the division; keep 2‑dp throughout.

exam.q: A map uses a scale of 1 cm : 250 m. A road on the map measures 3.6 cm. Find the real length of the road in kilometres.
model: Total parts = 1+250 = 251 (but we only need the conversion).
Real length = 3.6 cm × 250 m = 900 m = 0.9 km.
exam.tip: Convert metres to kilometres at the end.

exam.q: The ratio of the lengths of two similar triangles is 3:7. If the smaller triangle has a perimeter of 54 cm, find the perimeter of the larger triangle.
model: Perimeter follows the same ratio as side lengths.
exam.tip: Remember that all linear dimensions of similar figures share the same ratio.

exam.q: A mixture contains liquid X and liquid Y in the ratio 4:9. If the mixture weighs 260 g, how much does liquid Y weigh?
exam.tip: Only calculate the required part if the question asks for one component.

exam.q: A car travels 150 km in the same time a bike travels 90 km. Find the ratio of the car's speed to the bike's speed.
exam.tip: Time cancels, so directly simplify the distance ratio.

exam.q: A total of 720 ml of a solution is to be divided into parts A, B and C in the ratio 2:3:5. Find the volume of part B.
exam.tip: Write down the total parts first; it avoids mistakes.

worked.q: A school fundraiser raises £1 200. The money is to be split between the sports club, the music club and the drama club in the ratio 5:3:2. How much does each club receive?
steps: Write the ratio 5:3:2 (already simplest).
Total parts = 5+3+2 = 10.
Sports club = 5 × £120 = £600.
Music club = 3 × £120 = £360.
Drama club = 2 × £120 = £240.

worked.q: A garden is to be planted with roses and daisies in the ratio 4:7. If there are 84 rose plants, how many daisies are there?
steps: Ratio 4:7 – roses correspond to the first term (4).
One part = 84 ÷ 4 = 21.
Daisies = 7 × 21 = 147.

worked.q: A recipe requires ingredients in the ratio 3:2:5 (flour:sugar:butter). You have 900 g of butter. Find the total mass of the mixture.
steps: Butter corresponds to the third term (5).
One part = 900 ÷ 5 = 180 g.

maths_aqa_f.2.11.summary: Ratio lets us compare lengths, areas and volumes directly, linking similarity of shapes and trigonometric ratios. By using scale factors we can move from a small model to a real object, and the same ideas underpin sine, cosine and tangent when comparing sides of similar right‑angled triangles. Mastering these connections gives a powerful toolkit for geometry, scaling problems and real‑world applications.

core.p: A ratio expresses how many times one quantity contains another. It is written as a:b, a/b or a : b and can be reduced to its simplest form.
bullets: Both terms must be in the same units before forming the ratio.
A ratio can be written as a fraction or with a colon.
Reducing a ratio means dividing both terms by their greatest common divisor.

callouts.p: The quantitative relationship between two numbers of the same kind, expressed as a:b, a/b or a : b.

core.p: When two shapes are similar, all corresponding lengths have the same scale factor k. Areas scale by k² and volumes by k³.
bullets: If length‑scale = k, then area‑scale = k².
If length‑scale = k, then volume‑scale = k³.
Similarity means equal angles and proportional sides.

callouts.p: Corresponding angles are equal and corresponding sides are in proportion.

fig.cap: Two similar triangles with scale factor k.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="20" y="40" width="120" height="80" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540"/> <text x="80" y="30" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Small triangle</text> <rect x="200" y="20" width="180" height="120" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/> <text x="290" y="10" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540" text-anchor="middle">Large triangle (k=1.5)</text> <line x1="80" y1="120" x2="80" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540"/> <text x="85" y="160" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">k</text> <line x1="290" y1="140" x2="290" y2="200" stroke="#1b2540"/> <text x="295" y="170" font-size="11" fill="#1b2540">k</text></svg>

core.p: To compare two lengths, write the ratio of the longer to the shorter and reduce it.
bullets: Measure both lengths in the same unit.
Form the ratio L₁:L₂.
Reduce by dividing both terms by their GCD.

callouts.p: If the ratio is greater than 1, the first quantity is larger.

core.p: Areas are compared by the ratio of their numerical values, but remember that if the shapes are similar the area ratio is the square of the length ratio.
bullets: Calculate each area in the same units (e.g., cm²).
Form the ratio A₁:A₂.
If shapes are similar, check that A₁/A₂ = (k)².

callouts.p: Do NOT square the ratio twice – only one squaring is needed for area.

core.p: For similar 3‑D shapes, the volume ratio equals the cube of the length ratio.
bullets: Find each volume in the same units (e.g., cm³).
Form V₁:V₂.
If shapes are similar, verify V₁/V₂ = (k)³.

callouts.p: Volume ratio = (length ratio)³ for similar solids.

core.p: In a right‑angled triangle, the ratios of sides (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) are the sine, cosine and tangent of the acute angle. These are essentially length ratios.
bullets: sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.
cos θ = adjacent / hypotenuse.
tan θ = opposite / adjacent.
All three are dimension‑less because the units cancel.

callouts.p: A ratio of two sides of a right‑angled triangle that defines sin, cos or tan of an acute angle.

core.h: Using Ratios to Find Missing Lengths
core.p: If two similar figures share a known scale factor, missing lengths can be found by multiplying or dividing by k.
bullets: Identify the known corresponding lengths.
Set up L₁ = k·L₂ (or L₂ = L₁/k).
Solve for the unknown.

callouts.p: Keep track of units – they cancel in the ratio.

core.h: Area and Volume from Length Ratio
core.p: When only the length ratio is given, you can instantly obtain area and volume ratios using the square and cube rules.
bullets: Given k, area ratio = k².
Given k, volume ratio = k³.
Useful for scaling models, maps and engineering drawings.

callouts.p: Length → Area: square the scale factor; Length → Volume: cube the scale factor.

core.h: Practical: Similar Triangles on a Map
core.p: Maps use a scale ratio (e.g., 1 cm : 100 m). This is a length ratio that lets you convert any measured distance on the map to a real‑world distance.
bullets: Read the map scale.
Measure the distance on the map.
Multiply by the scale factor to get the real distance.

callouts.p: A ratio that relates a distance on a map to the corresponding distance on the ground.

core.p: Two right‑angled triangles that share an acute angle are similar; therefore their side ratios (sin, cos, tan) are equal.
bullets: If ∠A = ∠A' then sin A = sin A', cos A = cos A', tan A = tan A'.
This allows you to solve for unknown sides using known trigonometric ratios.

callouts.p: Do not confuse the ratio of sides with the numeric value of the angle.

analogy.p: Think of a recipe as a small model of a meal. If you double every ingredient (length ratio = 2), the total volume of the soup becomes eight times larger because volume scales with the cube of the length ratio. The analogy breaks down when ingredients do not scale uniformly (e.g., spices), just as geometric similarity requires all dimensions to change by the same factor.

terms.d: A quantitative relationship between two numbers of the same kind, expressed as a:b, a/b or a : b.
The constant multiplier that relates corresponding lengths of similar figures.
A relationship where two shapes have equal angles and proportional sides.
Two quantities are proportional if their ratio is constant.
A ratio of two sides of a right‑angled triangle defining sin, cos or tan of an acute angle.
A ratio that relates a distance on a map to the corresponding real‑world distance.
The ratio of two areas; for similar figures it equals the square of the length scale factor.
The ratio of two volumes; for similar solids it equals the cube of the length scale factor.
The side opposite the right angle in a right‑angled triangle.
The side opposite the angle of interest in a right‑angled triangle.
The side next to the angle of interest, not the hypotenuse.
A quantity without units, such as a ratio of like units.

mistakes.r: sin θ = opposite / hypotenuse.

mistakes.w: I used different units for the two lengths in a ratio.

worked.q: A small cone has radius 4 cm and height 6 cm. A larger cone is similar with radius 10 cm. Find its height.

maths_aqa_f.2.6.summary: Proportion exists when two ratios are equal to one another, forming equivalent multiplicative relationships between quantities. At AQA GCSE Foundation level, understanding proportion as equality of ratios allows students to solve missing value problems, scale recipes, convert currencies, and test whether two quantities maintain a constant proportional relationship. By writing ratios as equivalent fractions or applying scale factors, any unknown quantity in a proportional pair can be determined accurately without additive errors.

core.h: 1. What is Proportion as Equality of Ratios?
core.p: In mathematics, **proportion** means that two pairs of values share the exact same **ratio**. When we say two quantities are in proportion, it means as one quantity scales by a multiplicative factor, the other quantity scales by the exact same multiplicative factor.
bullets: A **ratio** compares two or more quantities (for example, 2 : 5).
A **proportion** is a statement that two ratios are equal (for example, 2 : 5 = 6 : 15).
If ratio A : B is equal to ratio C : D, then the fraction A / B is equal to the fraction C / D.
Proportional relationships are strictly **multiplicative**, never additive.

callouts.p: Proportion is an equation stating that two ratios are equal. If a : b = c : d, then the two pairs of values (a, b) and (c, d) are in direct proportion.
Adding the same amount to both sides of a ratio changes the ratio. Only multiplying or dividing both sides by the same non-zero number keeps the ratios equal.

core.p: Just like fractions, ratios can be written in **simplest form** by dividing all parts by their **highest common factor (HCF)**. Two ratios are equal if they simplify to the exact same simplest form.
bullets: To check if two ratios are equal, simplify both to their simplest whole-number form.
Example: 4 : 10 simplifies to 2 : 5 (divide by 2), and 12 : 30 simplifies to 2 : 5 (divide by 6).
Because both simplify to 2 : 5, the ratio 4 : 10 is equal to 12 : 30.
If two ratios simplify to different simplest forms, they are **not** in proportion.

callouts.p: Always simplify ratios fully before comparing them. If the simplified forms match, the quantities are directly proportional.

core.h: 3. Expressing Equal Ratios as Equivalent Fractions
core.p: Every ratio a : b can be expressed as a fraction a / b (or b / a). Setting two ratios as equal creates an **algebraic proportion equation** that can be solved easily.
bullets: If a : b = c : d, then a / b = c / d.
Alternatively, b / a = d / c (flipping both fractions maintains equality).
This allows missing values to be found by setting up a fraction equation and isolating the unknown variable.
For example, if 3 : 7 = x : 28, then 3 / 7 = x / 28.

callouts.p: Writing a : b = c : d as a/b = c/d makes it straightforward to solve for an unknown using standard linear equation methods.

core.h: 4. Finding Missing Values Using Scale Factors (Horizontal Multipliers)
core.p: When two ratios are equal, there is a constant **scale factor** (horizontal multiplier) that links the corresponding terms of the first ratio to the second ratio.
bullets: Identify the known pair of corresponding values across the two ratios.
Calculate the multiplier: **Scale Factor = New Value / Original Value**.
Multiply the remaining term in the first ratio by this scale factor to find the missing value.
Example: If 4 : 9 = 20 : x, the multiplier from 4 to 20 is 20 / 4 = 5. Therefore, x = 9 * 5 = 45.

callouts.p: Always divide the new value by the original corresponding value to find the exact multiplier. Works for integers and decimals.

core.p: Besides horizontal multipliers between ratios, there is an **internal relationship** (vertical multiplier) within each ratio that remains constant.
bullets: In the ratio a : b, the value of b is always a fixed multiple of a (b / a).
If a : b = c : d, then the ratio b / a must equal d / c.
Example: In 3 : 12 = 5 : x, notice that 12 is 4 times 3 (12 / 3 = 4).
Applying the same internal multiplier to the second ratio gives x = 5 * 4 = 20.

callouts.p: You can scale across ratios (Horizontal: ratio 1 -> ratio 2) or scale within ratios (Vertical: term 1 -> term 2). Both give the exact same answer.

core.p: Cross-multiplication is a universal algebraic technique derived directly from equality of fractions. If two ratios are equal, their cross-products are equal.
bullets: If **a / b = c / d**, then multiplying both sides by b * d yields **a * d = b * c**.
To find an unknown x in a / b = x / d, use: **x = (a * d) / b**.
Example: Solve 5 / 8 = x / 24.

callouts.p: Only use cross-multiplication when an equals sign exists between two fractions (a/b = c/d). Do NOT cross-multiply when multiplying fractions together!

core.h: 7. Using Ratio Tables to Solve Proportion Problems
core.p: A **ratio table** organizes proportional quantities into rows and columns, making it easy to perform step-by-step scaling using equal ratios.
bullets: Columns represent distinct quantities (e.g., Flour in grams, Sugar in grams).
Rows represent equivalent proportional states.
You can multiply or divide any row by a constant to produce a new valid row.
You can add or subtract corresponding values from two rows to find another proportional pair.

callouts.p: Ratio tables prevent arithmetic mistakes in multi-step non-calculator questions by breaking complex scaling down into simpler doubling, halving, or dividing by 10 steps.

core.h: 8. Testing Whether Two Quantities are in Proportion
core.p: A common AQA Foundation exam question asks whether two given pairs of quantities are in proportion. You must prove whether their ratios are equal.
bullets: **Method 1 (Simplest Form):** Write both pairs as ratios and simplify both completely. If they match, they are in proportion.
**Method 2 (Decimals / Unit Rate):** Calculate value 2 / value 1 for both sets. If the quotients are identical, they are in proportion.
**Method 3 (Cross-Products):** For pairs (a, b) and (c, d), check if a * d = b * c.
Always write a explicit concluding sentence (e.g., '3/4 = 3/4 so the quantities are in proportion').

callouts.p: Two variables y and x are in direct proportion if the ratio y : x (or quotient y/x) remains constant for all pairs of values.

core.p: Recipe questions are classic ratio equality applications where ingredients must be scaled up or down in exact proportion to the number of portions.
bullets: Set up the proportion: **(Original Ingredient) / (Original Servings) = (New Ingredient) / (New Servings)**.
Solve for the unknown new ingredient quantity.
Example: A recipe for 4 people requires 250g of butter. How much butter is needed for 10 people?

callouts.p: Alternatively, find the amount needed for 1 portion first (250 / 4 = 62.5g), then multiply by the new number of portions (62.5 * 10 = 625g).

core.h: 10. Currency Exchange Rates as Equal Ratios
core.p: Currency conversions rely entirely on equality of ratios between two currencies.
bullets: An exchange rate gives the base ratio: £1 = €1.15 (written as ratio 1 : 1.15).
To convert £240 into Euros, set up equal ratios: 1 : 1.15 = 240 : E.
Using horizontal scaling: E = 240 * 1.15 = €276.
To convert back from Euros to Pounds, divide by the unit rate multiplier.

callouts.p: Check your units! If £1 = €1.15, Pounds to Euros requires multiplying by 1.15. Euros to Pounds requires dividing by 1.15.

core.p: The single most common mark-losing mistake in GCSE Foundation ratio questions is applying **additive reasoning** instead of **multiplicative reasoning**.
bullets: Incorrect Additive Logic: 'If 3 : 5 becomes 7 : ?, I added 4 to the left, so I add 4 to the right to get 9.' (WRONG!)
Correct Multiplicative Logic: 'If 3 : 5 becomes 7 : ?, I multiplied the left by 7/3, so I multiply the right by 7/3 to get 35/3 = 11.67.' (CORRECT!)
Always remember: Proportions stay equal ONLY under multiplication and division.

callouts.t: Exam Alert: Spotting the Additive Trap
callouts.p: When a question gives a scenario like 'In 2020 the ratio of boys to girls was 4:5...', never assume adding equal numbers of boys and girls keeps the ratio equal!

analogy.p: Understanding proportion as equality of ratios is like resizing a digital photo. If an image is 400 pixels wide by 300 pixels high (ratio 4 : 3) and you resize it to 800 pixels wide, the height MUST scale by the exact same multiplier to 600 pixels (ratio 8 : 6 = 4 : 3). If you instead added 400 pixels to both dimensions (800 by 700), the ratio changes (8 : 7) and the image becomes stretched and distorted. The analogy breaks down because image resizing software deals with pixel rounding, whereas mathematical ratio equality is perfectly exact to infinite decimal places.

terms.d: A mathematical comparison of two or more quantities showing their relative sizes.
A statement or equation proving that two ratios or fractions are equal.
Ratios that express the same proportional relationship and simplify to the same simplest form.
The multiplier used to scale one ratio up or down to produce an equal ratio.
The algebraic process of setting diagonal products equal (a*d = b*c) when solving a/b = c/d.
Solving a proportion problem by first calculating the value corresponding to a single unit (1).
A ratio written with the smallest possible whole numbers having no common factors other than 1.
The largest whole number that divides into two or more numbers without leaving a remainder.
A relationship between two variables where their ratio remains constant; as one increases, the other increases at the same rate.
A structured table used to organize quantities and scale them proportionally step by step.
A connection between quantities based on multiplication or division, rather than addition or subtraction.
The ratio between two currencies specifying how much of one currency equals another.

mistakes.w: Adding the same amount to both sides of a ratio (e.g., 3:5 = (3+2):(5+2) = 5:7).
mistakes.r: Ratios are multiplicative. You must multiply both sides by the same factor (e.g., 3:5 = (3*2):(5*2) = 6:10).

mistakes.w: Writing 3 : 5 as the fraction 3/5 when trying to find the fraction of the total.
mistakes.r: 3 : 5 means 3 parts out of 8 total parts (3/8), but as a direct ratio comparison of part-to-part, 3/5 represents the ratio equal to 3:5.

mistakes.w: Flipping one side of a proportion equation when setting up equal fractions (e.g., writing a/b = d/c instead of a/b = c/d).
mistakes.r: Keep order consistent: if numerator is quantity A and denominator is quantity B on the left, keep quantity A on top and quantity B on bottom on the right.

mistakes.w: Dividing by the wrong number when finding the scale factor (e.g., doing Old / New instead of New / Old).
mistakes.r: Scale factor = New Value ÷ Original Value.

mistakes.w: Confusing direct proportion with inverse proportion when scaling recipes or speeds.
mistakes.r: Check context: if double the workers take half the time, that is inverse proportion; if double the guests require double the ingredients, that is direct proportion (equal ratios).

mistakes.w: Rounding intermediate scale factors too early, leading to incorrect final answers.
mistakes.r: Keep scale factors as exact fractions (e.g., 7/3) or store full decimals in your calculator until the final answer.

mistakes.w: Stating two ratios are equal without showing simplified forms or calculations.
mistakes.r: Always show working: simplify both ratios to simplest form or show equal decimal quotients to score full method marks.

mistakes.w: In currency questions, multiplying by the rate when you should divide.
mistakes.r: Set up the ratio 1 : rate = target : x and solve systematically using cross-multiplication or scale factor.

exam.q: Show that the ratio 12 : 18 is equal to the ratio 20 : 30.
model: Both ratios simplify to 2 : 3, so they are equal.
exam.tip: Simplify both ratios fully to their simplest whole-number form to show equality clearly.

exam.q: The ratios 4 : 7 and 16 : x are equal. Work out the value of x.
exam.tip: Find the multiplier between the corresponding terms first.

exam.q: Are the ratios 5 : 8 and 15 : 22 equal? You must show working to justify your answer.
exam.tip: State clearly whether they are equal or not after showing your mathematical evidence.

exam.q:
Here are the ingredients to make 8 pancakes:
- 100g flour
- 200ml milk
- 1 egg

Work out how much flour is needed to make 12 pancakes.
exam.tip: Scale factor = target portions divided by original portions.

exam.q:
A shop sells red paint and blue paint mixed in the ratio 3 : 5.
In a larger tin of the same colour mix, there are 35 litres of blue paint.
Work out how many litres of red paint are in the larger tin.
exam.tip: Identify which part of the ratio corresponds to the given value.

exam.q:
In Store A, 6 pens cost £4.50.
In Store B, 10 pens cost £7.20.
Are the prices in Store A and Store B proportional to the number of pens? Show working.
model: Store A unit price: £4.50 / 6 = £0.75 per pen
Store B unit price: £7.20 / 10 = £0.72 per pen
The ratio of cost to pens is 4.50:6 = 0.75:1 for Store A and 7.20:10 = 0.72:1 for Store B.
Because the unit prices (ratios) are not equal, the prices are not proportional.
exam.tip: Calculate unit rate (cost per 1 pen) for both to compare ratios easily.

exam.q: Solve the proportion equation: 5 / 9 = x / 45.
model: Multiplier from denominator 9 to denominator 45 is 45 / 9 = 5
exam.tip: You can use scale factors or cross-multiplication (5 * 45 = 9 * x -> 225 = 9x -> x = 25).

exam.q: Using the exchange rate £1 = $1.30, convert $390 into Pounds (£).
exam.tip: Dividing dollars by 1.30 gives the equivalent amount in pounds.

exam.q:
A map has a scale where 2 cm represents 5 km.
On the map, the distance between two towns is 7 cm.
Calculate the real-life distance in km.
model: Set up equal ratios: 2 cm : 5 km = 7 cm : x km
exam.tip: Write the map scale as a ratio 2 : 5 and scale horizontally by 3.5.

worked.q: A cake recipe for 6 people requires 180g of sugar and 240g of flour. Ben wants to adapt the recipe for 15 people. Calculate the amount of sugar and flour Ben needs.
steps: Step 1: Identify the scaling factor between original people and target people.
Scale factor = target servings / original servings = 15 / 6 = 2.5
Step 2: Apply the scale factor to the sugar quantity using equal ratios (180 : 6 = Sugar : 15).
Sugar needed = 180g * 2.5 = 450g
Step 3: Apply the scale factor to the flour quantity using equal ratios (240 : 6 = Flour : 15).
Flour needed = 240g * 2.5 = 600g
worked.ans: Ben needs 450g of sugar and 600g of flour.

worked.q: Two rectangles are mathematically similar. Rectangle A has width 6 cm and height 15 cm. Rectangle B has width 14 cm and height h cm. Using the equality of side ratios, work out the value of h.
steps: Step 1: Set up the ratio equality of width to height for both rectangles.
Width A : Height A = Width B : Height B -> 6 : 15 = 14 : h
Step 2: Express as equivalent fractions.
Step 3: Simplify the left fraction.
6 / 15 simplifies to 2 / 5
Step 4: Solve 2 / 5 = 14 / h using scale factor.
